newsitem.title: USA: Tucker's Whitewater trial postponed indefinitely.
newsitem.headline: Tucker's Whitewater trial postponed indefinitely.

text.p: A federal judge Tuesday postponed indefinitely the second Whitewater trial of former Arkansas Gov. Jim Guy Tucker, saying he was too sick to go through another prosecution.

In a setback for Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr, U.S. District Judge Stephen Reasoner said he was persuaded by doctors' opinions that Tucker, who had a liver transplant late last year, was unable to face the bankruptcy fraud trial scheduled for September.
"Having been warned by these doctors, the Court wishes to avoid the possible specter of Mr. Tucker rejecting his transplanted liver during the middle of trial," Reasoner said in his ruling.

Starr had submitted a written brief opposing a delay, and sought a hearing at which he said government doctors would testify that Tucker's recovery from transplant surgery was satisfactory and would not prevent a September trial.
But Reasoner said he was "satisfied that defendant Tucker's health is precarious."
Tucker and two other men are accused of conspiring to violate bankruptcy laws and avoid taxes from the sale of a cable television system during the 1980s. All three men have pleaded not guilty.
Tucker was convicted in May 1996 on fraud charges in the first Whitewater trial.
His fellow defendants in the case were James and Susan McDougal, former business partners of President Clinton in the ill-fated Whitewater real estate project.
The McDougals were both sentenced to prison, but Tucker escaped jail time because of his life-threatening liver problem and was instead given four years probation with 18 years home detention.

Susan McDougal told CNN's "Crossfire" programme Tuesday she would rather serve out her 18-month prison sentence for civil contempt than testify before the Whitewater Grand Jury since she believed it was a biased body that was "not interested in the truth".

But McDougal, 42, who is being held in isolation at Twin Towers Correctional Facility in Los Angeles after refusing to cooperate with Starr's wide-ranging probe, said she would testify in open court where Americans could form their own opinions about her story.
McDougal's ex-husband is cooperating with prosecutors but she has refused, saying Starr is waging a vendetta against Clinton and wants her to lie about the President.

Both cases against Tucker were brought as part of Starr's ongoing Whitewater investigation, which began as a probe into Clinton's personal and political finances but has widened to include several Arkansas political and business figures who had little or nothing to do with Clinton.
Tucker became state governor when Clinton won the 1992 presidential election and went to the White House, but the two men were never close friends or business partners.
Tucker resigned after his fraud conviction last year.
